chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from one of his companions, from Umar ibn Yazeed, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'A Hajj is superior to freeing seventy necks.' So I said, 'Does anything equate to the Hajj?' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Nothing equates to it, and for one Dirham in the Hajj is superior to two million Dirhams in what is besides it.'

From the Ways of Allah. Then he (peace be upon him) said to him: 'I went out upon more than seventy camels and some ten animals, and I had bought black slaves to increase the number with them, and the eating of vinegar and oil had harmed me until Hameeda instructed that a chicken be grilled, so I returned to my former self.'

key_terms.إِهْرَامٌ: State of consecration for Hajj (implied by context of dietary restriction)
key_terms.سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ: The Way of Allah (general term for acts of worship/charity)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual merit of Hajj compared to other acts of worship according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes the preeminence of Hajj by declaring that even a single Dirham spent on it outweighs two million Dirhams in other acts of worship, highlighting its unique spiritual weight. He illustrates the physical discipline required by recounting his own journey with a large caravan, noting how the strict dietary restrictions of Ihram—specifically the aversion to vinegar and oil—were so intense that he only regained his appetite after breaking his fast with grilled chicken. This narration underscores the comprehensive nature of Hajj, where physical sacrifice and financial expenditure are transformed into superior spiritual merit.
